title: Ocean Explorer: Dive for the Planet
description: Dive into the deep blue! Navigate a 20-tile ocean expedition as a marine biologist exploring coral reefs, rescuing sea creatures, and fighting ocean pollution. Make conservation decisions that affect marine ecosystems, buy diving equipment at underwater shops, and face boss challenges from the ocean's toughest problems. Your mission: reach the Ocean Guardian finish line with maximum knowledge, eco score, and equipment!
learning_objectives: Learn about marine ecosystems, coral reefs, and ocean biodiversity
Understand the impact of pollution, overfishing, and climate change on oceans
Explore conservation strategies and sustainable ocean practices
Develop environmental decision-making skills through scenario-based choices

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Roll the dice to navigate your marine biologist along the ocean expedition board
Land on Ocean Discovery tiles to learn about marine life and earn Knowledge Points
Visit the Dive Equipment Shop to spend Knowledge Points on gear like cameras and coral repair kits
Face Ocean Challenge tiles where you must answer conservation questions correctly
Reach the Ocean Guardian finish tile with the highest Eco Score and Knowledge Points to win
tips: Collect Knowledge Points early -- you need them to buy crucial equipment at shop tiles
Upgrading your equipment level helps you handle tougher challenges in deeper waters
Read each ocean event carefully -- the right conservation choice boosts both knowledge and eco score

challenge.question: A massive oil spill is spreading towards a coral reef. What is the most effective FIRST response?
options: Deploy floating barriers (booms) to contain the spill before it reaches the reef
Wait for the oil to dissolve naturally in the ocean
Use chemical dispersants only -- they break up oil instantly
Evacuate the area and close the beach
challenge.success_message: Excellent! Containment booms are the critical first step to stop the spread. You saved the reef!
challenge.fail_message: Not quite. Containment should always come first -- every minute the spill spreads, more marine life is affected.
challenge.explanation: Deploying floating barriers (booms) is the correct first response to an oil spill because containment must happen before cleanup. Booms physically prevent oil from spreading to sensitive areas like coral reefs. Waiting for natural dissolution is ineffective -- crude oil persists for years. Chemical dispersants break oil into smaller droplets that sink and harm seabed life. Evacuating beaches addresses human safety but does nothing to protect the marine ecosystem from the spreading oil.

evt_turtle_rescue.title: Sea Turtle Tangled in Fishing Net!
evt_turtle_rescue.story: A young Olive Ridley sea turtle -- the same species that nests on India's Odisha coast every year -- is trapped in an abandoned fishing net. It's struggling to breathe. The net is tangled around its flippers and shell. Thousands of sea turtles die from ghost nets every year.

choices.text: Carefully cut the net away using your dive knife, then document it for the marine authority
choices.feedback: Perfect approach! You freed the turtle safely and reported the ghost net. Your documentation helps authorities track illegal fishing zones. The turtle swims away, flippers free!

choices.text: Pull the net off quickly and release the turtle immediately
choices.feedback: The turtle is free, which is great! But pulling hastily could injure its flippers. Also, without documentation, the ghost net problem continues. Next time, be gentle and report it.

choices.text: Take photos for social media awareness but don't touch the turtle
choices.feedback: Awareness matters, but the turtle needed immediate help! In wildlife rescue, direct action comes first, documentation second. The turtle may not survive the wait.

evt_turtle_rescue.reflection_prompt: When you encounter an animal in distress, what is the balance between acting immediately and acting carefully? How does documentation help future animals even though it slows down the rescue of the one in front of you?

evt_coral_survey.title: Coral Reef Bleaching Alert
evt_coral_survey.story: The coral reef here is showing signs of bleaching -- once-vibrant corals have turned ghostly white. Coral bleaching happens when ocean temperatures rise, causing corals to expel the algae living in their tissues. Without these algae, corals starve. India's Gulf of Mannar and Lakshadweep reefs are facing this crisis.

choices.text: Deploy your coral repair kit to transplant healthy coral fragments onto the damaged reef
choices.feedback: Brilliant conservation work! Coral gardening -- transplanting healthy fragments -- is one of the most effective reef restoration methods. Scientists in Lakshadweep are doing exactly this. Your eco score soars!

choices.text: Set up underwater temperature monitors and map the bleaching extent for researchers
choices.feedback: Excellent scientific approach! Long-term monitoring data is crucial for understanding bleaching patterns. Your data will help marine biologists predict and prevent future bleaching events.

choices.text: It's natural -- corals recover on their own. Continue your dive.
choices.feedback: Unfortunately, this isn't just natural variation. Human-caused climate change has accelerated bleaching to levels corals can't recover from. Without intervention, this reef could die within years.

evt_deep_sea.title: Bioluminescent Deep Sea Discovery!
evt_deep_sea.story: At 1000 metres deep, you enter the Twilight Zone. Suddenly, the darkness explodes with blue and green lights! Bioluminescent creatures -- anglerfish, jellyfish, and tiny dinoflagellates -- light up the abyss. Over 80% of deep-sea creatures produce their own light. India's Arabian Sea has rich deep-sea biodiversity yet to be fully explored!

choices.text: Collect water samples and photograph the creatures for scientific research cataloguing
choices.feedback: Incredible data collection! Your samples reveal three species not yet catalogued in Indian Ocean databases. Deep-sea research is the new frontier -- we know more about the Moon's surface than our ocean floor!

choices.text: Float silently and observe their natural behaviour without disturbing them
choices.feedback: Respectful observation! You notice the anglerfish uses its bioluminescent lure to attract prey, while the jellyfish flashes to confuse predators. Sometimes the best science is just watching.

evt_shark_encounter.title: Whale Shark -- Gentle Giant of the Sea!
evt_shark_encounter.story: A 12-metre whale shark glides gracefully towards you! Despite being the world's largest fish, whale sharks are gentle filter feeders that eat plankton. India's Gujarat coast (Saurashtra) is a major whale shark habitat. Local fishermen once hunted them, but conservation programmes have turned fishermen into whale shark protectors!

choices.text: Carefully attach a satellite tracking tag to study its migration patterns
choices.feedback: Valuable research! Satellite tags have revealed that whale sharks travel thousands of kilometres across oceans. Your data helps create protected marine corridors for their migration routes.

choices.text: Swim alongside it at a safe distance and record its feeding behaviour
choices.feedback: What a magical experience! You observe the whale shark filtering 6000 litres of water per hour through its gills. Maintaining distance shows respect for wildlife -- the golden rule of marine encounters.

choices.text: Try to touch its skin to feel the famous dermal denticles
choices.feedback: Touching wildlife stresses them and can damage their protective mucus layer! Marine biologists always observe from a respectful distance. The whale shark veers away, startled.

evt_plastic_pollution.title: The Great Plastic Patch
evt_plastic_pollution.story: You've entered a floating island of plastic waste -- bottles, bags, wrappers, microplastics. India generates 3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually. In the ocean, plastic breaks into microplastics that are eaten by fish, which are then eaten by humans. A recent study found microplastics in 80% of tested fish from the Indian coast.

choices.text: Organize an underwater cleanup -- collect and bag the waste for proper disposal on shore
choices.feedback: Hero move! You collect 15 kg of plastic in one dive session. Every piece removed is one less threat to marine life. Your effort inspires local fishing communities to join beach cleanup drives!

choices.text: Document the pollution with photos and GPS coordinates, then report to environmental authorities
choices.feedback: Strategic approach! Your documented evidence helps authorities trace the pollution source to illegal dumping upstream. The data becomes part of India's National Marine Litter Action Plan.

choices.text: Collect water samples to test microplastic concentration levels for research
choices.feedback: Critical research! Your samples reveal alarming microplastic levels -- 150 particles per litre. This data gets published in a marine science journal and influences policy change.

evt_plastic_pollution.reflection_prompt: Cleaning up plastic addresses the symptom, while documenting and reporting addresses the cause. In environmental conservation, when should you focus on immediate action versus systemic change? Can one person's cleanup really make a difference?

evt_overfishing.title: Illegal Trawling Nets Detected!
evt_overfishing.story: Your sonar picks up illegal bottom-trawling nets dragging across the seabed, destroying everything in their path -- corals, sponges, juvenile fish. Bottom trawling is like bulldozing a forest to catch a few birds. India banned trawling during monsoon breeding season, but enforcement is weak.

choices.text: Radio the Indian Coast Guard with GPS coordinates and photographic evidence
choices.feedback: Swift and effective! The Coast Guard dispatches a patrol vessel. The illegal trawlers are caught and fined. Your evidence strengthens the case for stricter fishing regulations.

choices.text: Deploy marker buoys around the affected area to warn other vessels and protect the zone
choices.feedback: Good protective action! The marker buoys create a temporary no-fishing zone. Local sustainable fishermen appreciate the effort and agree to help patrol the area.

evt_overfishing.reflection_prompt: Reporting illegal fishing to authorities could put you in conflict with local communities that depend on fishing for survival. How do you balance environmental enforcement with empathy for people's livelihoods? What does sustainable fishing look like in practice?

evt_dolphin_pod.title: Playful Dolphin Pod!
evt_dolphin_pod.story: A pod of 20 Indo-Pacific Humpback Dolphins surrounds your boat! These dolphins are found along India's western coast, especially near Mumbai and Goa. They're highly intelligent -- they use echolocation to hunt, communicate with clicks and whistles, and even have individual 'names' (signature whistles)! Sadly, they're classified as 'Vulnerable' due to coastal development and pollution.

choices.text: Lower a hydrophone to record their communication patterns for bioacoustics research
choices.feedback: Fascinating recordings! You capture 12 distinct signature whistles, suggesting this pod has at least 12 unique individuals. Your acoustic data helps researchers track this pod's health over time.

choices.text: Cut your boat engine and let them approach naturally -- observe their social behaviour
choices.feedback: Respectful choice! With the engine off, the dolphins relax and show natural behaviour -- mothers teaching calves to hunt, juveniles playing, the pod moving in coordinated formation. This is conservation through respect.

choices.text: Toss fish to attract them closer for better observation
choices.feedback: Never feed wild dolphins! It makes them dependent on humans, changes their natural hunting behaviour, and draws them dangerously close to boats. Several dolphins are injured by boat propellers each year because of this.

evt_oil_spill_boss.title: BOSS: Oil Spill Emergency!
evt_oil_spill_boss.story: A massive oil tanker has run aground near a pristine coral reef. Thousands of litres of crude oil are leaking into the sea. This is one of the worst environmental disasters in the region. Marine life is in immediate danger -- sea birds are coated in oil, fish are suffocating, and the coral is being smothered. As a marine biologist, you must lead the emergency response!

choices.text: Deploy floating containment booms to stop the spread, then coordinate skimmer boats for oil recovery
choices.feedback: Outstanding crisis management! Containment first, cleanup second -- exactly what the Indian Coast Guard manual recommends. Your quick action saved 80% of the reef from oil contact.
choices.explanation: Containment booms are the internationally recognized first response to marine oil spills because they physically stop the spread of oil. Once contained, skimmer boats can recover the oil from the surface. Chemical dispersants and in-situ burning are secondary options with significant environmental trade-offs. The Indian Coast Guard protocol follows exactly this sequence: contain, skim, then evaluate further options.

choices.text: Spray chemical dispersants from aircraft to break up the oil slick quickly
choices.feedback: Dispersants work but they're controversial -- they break oil into smaller droplets that sink to the seabed, potentially harming bottom-dwelling organisms. It's a trade-off: surface clean but seabed polluted.

choices.text: Set the surface oil on fire (controlled in-situ burning) to remove it quickly
choices.feedback: In-situ burning produces toxic smoke and leaves behind heavy residues that sink. While sometimes used in open ocean, near a reef it causes additional damage to marine life through air pollution and residue.

evt_warming_boss.title: BOSS: Ocean Warming Crisis!
evt_warming_boss.story: Alert! Ocean temperatures in this region have risen 2 degrees Celsius above normal. Mass coral bleaching is underway -- 60% of the reef has turned ghostly white. Fish populations are migrating to cooler waters, disrupting the entire food chain. The Indian Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean basin. You must devise a response strategy!

choices.text: Deploy experimental coral shade structures and establish a marine protected cooling zone
choices.feedback: Innovative thinking! Shade structures (like those tested on the Great Barrier Reef) can reduce bleaching by 30%. Combined with protected zones, this gives corals the best chance to recover naturally.
choices.explanation: Coral shade structures reduce direct sunlight and lower localized water temperatures, cutting bleaching rates by up to 30%. Combined with a marine protected zone that limits human activity, this gives corals the best chance to recover their symbiotic algae naturally. This approach is proactive yet minimally invasive, unlike relocation which is more disruptive, or passive documentation which allows continued degradation.

choices.text: Begin emergency coral relocation -- transplant the healthiest specimens to deeper, cooler waters
choices.feedback: Assisted migration is a cutting-edge conservation strategy! Scientists at ICAR are doing exactly this in Lakshadweep. You've saved hundreds of heat-tolerant coral genotypes for future reef rebuilding.

choices.text: Focus only on documenting the bleaching for research -- intervention is too risky
choices.feedback: While documentation is valuable, the crisis demands action! Without intervention, the entire reef could die within months. Climate change waits for no one -- every degree matters.

evt_tsunami_boss.title: BOSS: Tsunami Warning -- Final Challenge!
evt_tsunami_boss.story: EMERGENCY! A 7.8 magnitude undersea earthquake has triggered a tsunami warning for coastal villages near your expedition zone. Waves could arrive in 45 minutes. You know these waters -- there are fishing boats at sea, a marine sanctuary nearby, and three coastal villages with no seawalls. The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning Centre has issued a RED ALERT. What's your priority?

choices.text: Activate the village early warning sirens and coordinate boat evacuation via marine radio
choices.feedback: HERO! Your immediate action saved lives. India's INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services) operates exactly this kind of warning network. Boats headed to deep water (safest place), villages evacuated to higher ground. Zero casualties!
choices.explanation: Human lives are always the top priority in any natural disaster. Activating early warning sirens and coordinating boat evacuation via marine radio directly addresses the most critical need -- getting people to safety before the waves arrive. India's INCOIS warning system exists precisely for this purpose. Securing research equipment or observing the wave, while tempting for a scientist, risks lives and violates the fundamental principle of disaster response: save people first.

choices.text: Rush to the marine sanctuary to secure critical research equipment and specimens
choices.feedback: You saved valuable research, but human lives must always come first in a disaster. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 230,000 people -- early warning systems are the most important tool we have.

choices.text: Head to a safe observation point to record the tsunami for scientific study
choices.feedback: NEVER approach a tsunami for observation! The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami taught us: when the sea recedes, RUN to higher ground. Scientists study tsunamis using seismographs and tide gauges, not by watching them.

evt_hydrothermal.title: Hydrothermal Vent -- Life Without Sunlight!
evt_hydrothermal.story: You've discovered a hydrothermal vent at 2500 metres deep! Superheated water (400 degrees Celsius) shoots out from cracks in the ocean floor, carrying minerals that support an entire ecosystem WITHOUT sunlight. Giant tube worms, blind shrimp, and heat-loving bacteria thrive here. India's National Institute of Oceanography discovered hydrothermal vents in the Indian Ocean's Carlsberg Ridge!

choices.text: Collect mineral and biological samples using your robotic arm for lab analysis
choices.feedback: Groundbreaking research! Your samples contain chemosynthetic bacteria that convert chemicals (not sunlight) into energy. These extremophiles could hold keys to understanding life on other planets and developing new medicines!

choices.text: Create a detailed 3D map of the vent ecosystem using sonar and cameras
choices.feedback: Excellent cartography! Your 3D map reveals the full extent of this vent field -- 200 metres of thriving deep-sea life. The map will be used to propose this area as a Marine Protected Area, shielding it from deep-sea mining.

win_conditions.description: Navigate all 20 tiles to reach the Ocean Guardian finish! Your success is measured by Knowledge Points, Eco Score, and Equipment Level. Make wise conservation choices to maximize your impact on the ocean!

glossary_terms.definition: When corals turn white because rising water temperatures cause them to expel the colourful algae (zooxanthellae) living inside them. Without these algae, corals slowly starve.
glossary_terms.example: The Great Barrier Reef experienced severe bleaching in 2016-2017 due to marine heatwaves.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Bleaching = corals lose their colourful roommates and go hungry!

glossary_terms.definition: The ability of living organisms to produce their own light through chemical reactions inside their bodies.
glossary_terms.example: Fireflies on land and anglerfish in the ocean both use bioluminescence.

glossary_terms.definition: Tiny plastic particles (less than 5mm) that result from larger plastics breaking down. They're now found in seafood, drinking water, and even human blood.
glossary_terms.example: A single plastic bottle can break into thousands of microplastic particles over time.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Micro = tiny, but tiny plastics cause MACRO problems!

glossary_terms.definition: A section of ocean where human activity is restricted to protect marine ecosystems, like a national park but underwater.
glossary_terms.example: India's Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park protects coral reefs, mangroves, and sea grass beds.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which organisms produce energy from chemical reactions instead of sunlight -- the opposite of photosynthesis.
glossary_terms.example: Bacteria near hydrothermal vents use hydrogen sulfide to produce energy, supporting entire ecosystems in total darkness.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Photo-synthesis uses light; Chemo-synthesis uses chemicals!

achievements.description: Collect samples from the hydrothermal vent

marine_ecosystem.definition: A complex web of living organisms and their physical environment in the ocean, from coral reefs to deep-sea vents.
marine_ecosystem.example: A coral reef ecosystem includes corals, fish, algae, and countless microorganisms working together.
marine_ecosystem.real_world_example: The Great Barrier Reef supports 1,500+ fish species and is visible from space.

ocean_conservation.definition: Protecting and preserving ocean ecosystems through reducing pollution, overfishing, and habitat destruction.
ocean_conservation.example: Establishing marine protected areas where fishing and mining are restricted.
ocean_conservation.real_world_example: The ban on single-use plastics in many countries aims to reduce the 8 million tons of plastic entering oceans yearly.

biodiversity.definition: The variety of life in a particular habitat or ecosystem. Higher biodiversity means greater ecosystem resilience.
biodiversity.example: A healthy forest has hundreds of plant species, insects, birds, and mammals coexisting.
biodiversity.real_world_example: The Amazon rainforest contains 10% of all known species on Earth.

climate_change.definition: Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, primarily driven by human activities like burning fossil fuels.
climate_change.example: Rising ocean temperatures cause coral bleaching, killing reef ecosystems.
climate_change.real_world_example: Arctic sea ice has declined by 13% per decade since 1979.

food_chain.definition: A linear sequence showing how energy flows from one organism to another through eating. Producers -> Consumers -> Decomposers.
food_chain.real_world_example: When shark populations decline, entire ocean food chains collapse as prey species overpopulate.

pollution.definition: Contamination of the ocean by harmful substances like plastic, oil, chemicals, and agricultural runoff.
pollution.example: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a floating island of plastic waste twice the size of Texas.
pollution.real_world_example: An estimated 1 million seabirds and 100,000 marine mammals die from plastic pollution every year.
